name: LT3094EMSE#TRPBF
title: LT3094: -20 V, 500 mA negative LDO regulator with ultralow noise and ultrahigh PSRR, MSOP-12 and 3 mm × 3 mm DFN-12
summary: The LT3094 is a negative low-dropout linear regulator for noise-sensitive loads: a 100 µA precision current into SET and a single resistor set the output anywhere from 0 V to -19.5 V, and a unity-gain buffer drives OUT, so noise, PSRR and bandwidth stay nearly constant over the output range. It runs from -1.8 V to -20 V, delivers 500 mA with 235 mV typical dropout, and reaches 0.8 µVRMS noise and 74 dB PSRR at 1 MHz with one capacitor across the SET resistor. It adds a bipolar enable/UVLO pin, programmable current limit, programmable power good with fast start-up, and a VIOC output that makes an upstream switcher track its output. It is stable with 10 µF ceramic output capacitance and parallels directly for more current.
key_figures: 0.8 µVRMS (10 Hz to 100 kHz), 2.2 nV/√Hz at 10 kHz

notes: #PBF is lead-free finish in tubes, #TRPBF the same on tape and reel; some packages also come in 500-unit reels with the suffix #TRMPBF. The grade letter (E, I, H, MP) is marked on the shipping container label, not on the part. Wider temperature ranges are available from the factory.

pins.name: IN
pins.function: Negative supply input; pins 1, 2 and the exposed pad 13 are all IN. Needs a bypass capacitor at the pin; 10 µF is usually enough, more where large load transients would make the supply droop. A battery's impedance climbs with frequency, so battery-fed designs need the capacitor too.

pins.name: IN
pins.function: Second IN pin, same node as pin 1.

pins.name: EN/UV
pins.function: Enable and undervoltage lockout. Low (near ground) shuts the part down to 3 µA and turns the output off. Bidirectional: the part turns on when the pin is about 1.26 V above ground (200 mV hysteresis falling) or about 1.26 V below ground (215 mV hysteresis). A divider from IN to EN/UV to GND sets an input UVLO. Tie to IN when not used; never leave it floating.

pins.name: PG
pins.function: Power good flag. Pulled low while PGFB sits between 0 V and -300 mV. Valid in shutdown, where it is held low. Leave floating if unused.

pins.name: PGFB
pins.function: Power good feedback. PG goes high once PGFB is below -300 mV on its rising edge, with 7 mV hysteresis falling. A divider OUT to PGFB to GND programs the threshold: -0.3 V • (1 + RPG1/RPG2) - IPGFB • RPG1. PGFB also turns on fast start-up. Tie to IN when neither power good nor fast start-up is wanted.

pins.name: ILIM
pins.function: Current limit programming. A resistor to GND sets the limit with a 3.75 A • kΩ scale factor; Kelvin-connect it to the GND pin for accuracy. Tie to GND when not used; never float it.

pins.name: VIOC
pins.function: Voltage for input-to-output control: output of a tracking amplifier that drives an upstream regulator's feedback to hold the drop across the LT3094 constant, for lower dissipation and better PSRR. Float it when not used.

pins.name: SET
pins.function: Inverting input of the error amplifier and the regulation set point. Sinks a precise 100 µA through a resistor to GND, so VSET = ISET • RSET; output range 0 V to -19.5 V. A capacitor SET to GND improves noise, PSRR and transient response and slows start-up unless fast start-up is used. Kelvin-connect the ground end of the SET resistor at the load.

pins.name: GND
pins.function: Ground.

pins.name: OUTS
pins.function: Output sense, the noninverting input of the error amplifier. Kelvin-connect to the output capacitor and the load, and join the grounds of the output and SET capacitors directly. A substrate diode runs from OUTS to IN: never drive OUTS more than 0.3 V below IN.

pins.name: OUT
pins.function: Regulator output (pins 11 and 12). Needs at least 10 µF with ESR below 30 mΩ and ESL below 1.5 nH; larger load steps need more capacitance. A substrate diode runs from OUT to IN: never drive OUT more than 0.3 V below IN.

pins.name: OUT
pins.function: Second OUT pin, same node as pin 11.

pins.name: IN
pins.function: Exposed pad, connected to IN; must be soldered to the PCB.

notes: Note 1: Operating past these limits can damage the part permanently; long exposure at any of them can shorten its life and reduce its reliability.
Note 2: EN/UV, ILIM, PG, PGFB, SET, GND, VIOC, OUTS and OUT each have a parasitic diode to IN. In a fault none of them may go more than 0.3 V below IN; in normal use each stays more positive than IN.
Note 4: SET and OUTS are clamped by diodes with two 400 Ω series resistors; for transients shorter than 5 ms the clamp can take more than the rated current.
Note 5: The SET and OUTS pin current limits must also be met.
Note 6: The OUT-to-OUTS limit is guaranteed by design.

Operating life shortens at high junction temperature and is derated above 125 °C.

Note 7: Maximum junction temperature limits the operating conditions, and current-limit foldback (which begins at VOUT - VIN > 7V) means regulation is not specified for every combination of input voltage and output current. At full output current keep the input range limited; at the highest input voltage keep the output current limited.
Note 8: The EN/UV threshold must be met for the part to operate.
Note 9: OUTS is connected straight to OUT.

Note 10: Dropout is the smallest input-to-output differential that keeps regulation at the given output current, taken where the output has fallen 1% out of regulation. This gives a higher figure than hard dropout, which is measured at VIN = VOUT(NOMINAL). From 0V to -1.8V output, dropout is limited by the minimum input voltage.

Note 11: GND pin current is measured with VIN = VOUT(NOMINAL) and a current-source load, so the part is in dropout; this is the worst case, and the current falls at higher input voltage. It excludes the SET and ILIM pin currents, which quiescent current includes.

Note 12: A capacitor across the SET resistor lowers output noise by bypassing that resistor's thermal noise and the reference current's noise, leaving the error amplifier's noise; it also lengthens start-up.
Note 13: The scale factor applies while the internal backup current limit is inactive. The internal limit folds back for VOUT - VIN beyond 7V.

Note 14: The internal backup current limit folds back, lowering the limit, for VOUT - VIN > 7V. Some output current is available at every differential; the current-limit curves against input-to-output differential give the values.
Note 15: The VIOC amplifier output equals VIN - VOUT, or VIN + 1.5V when VOUT lies between 0V and -1.5V.
Note 16: Between 0V and -1.5V output, a 10µA minimum load is needed for stability.

circuits.title: Typical application: -5 V to -3.3 V at 500 mA
circuits.description: A -5 V supply regulated to -3.3 V for loads up to 500 mA. RSET (33.2 kΩ) carries the 100 µA SET current, giving -3.32 V at SET and at the output; CSET (4.7 µF) across it lowers noise and raises PSRR. RILIM (7.5 kΩ) programs a 500 mA current limit. The 450 kΩ / 50 kΩ divider from OUT puts the power good threshold at -3.0 V, and PG is pulled up to a 3.3 V rail through 200 kΩ. EN/UV is tied to IN so the part runs whenever the input is present. OUTS joins OUT at the output capacitor.
notes: VIOC is left unconnected.

circuits.title: Basic adjustable regulator (Figure 1)
circuits.description: One resistor from SET to ground sets the output: 33.2 kΩ gives -3.3 V from a -5 V input, with 4.7 µF across it for low noise. ILIM goes straight to ground, so only the internal current limit acts. PGFB and EN/UV both go to IN, which keeps the part on and leaves fast start-up and power good off. A 10 µF capacitor sits on the output and a bypass capacitor on the input.
notes: PG and VIOC are left unconnected.

circuits.title: COUT and CSET connections for best performance (Figure 3)
circuits.description: The basic regulator wired as four-terminal connections to the output capacitor: OUTS runs on its own trace to the live side of COUT, and the ground ends of RSET and CSET run to the ground side of COUT rather than to the GND pin, while GND and ILIM share their own ground. Electrically the grounds are one node; the separate runs keep trace resistance and inductance out of the sensing.
notes: PG and VIOC are left unconnected.

circuits.title: Typical VIOC application (Figure 7)
circuits.description: An upstream switching converter feeds the LT3094 input (VLDOIN) through its inductor. VIOC drives the converter's feedback node through R2, with R1 from that node to ground, so the converter's output follows the LT3094 output and the drop across the LDO stays at VFBSWITCHER • (R1 + R2) / R1. Optional R3 from VLDOIN to VIOC caps the converter output if SET opens. EN/UV and PGFB go to IN. A variable resistor with 4.7 µF across it sets a variable output; 10 µF on the output, 500 mA maximum.
notes: ILIM and PG have no connection in this circuit.
Inside the part VIOC has about 40 kΩ to GND.

circuits.title: VIOC connection using LT8330 (Figure 8)
circuits.description: An LT8330 wired as an inverting converter with a coupled inductor feeds the LT3094 input. From the LT3094 IN, 86.6 kΩ (R3) goes to VIOC, 9.53 kΩ (R2) from VIOC to the LT8330 FBX pin, and 38.3 kΩ (R1) from FBX to ground. With FBX at -0.8 V the converter output is -4.3 V while the LT3094 makes -3.3 V (VIOC at -1 V), and -5 V when the LT3094 is disabled.
notes: The LT3094 pins other than IN and VIOC are not part of this circuit.

circuits.title: VIOC connection using LT8580 (Figure 9)
circuits.description: An LT8580 inverting converter feeds the LT3094 input. Its FBX pin regulates at 3 mV with 83.3 µA flowing out, so one resistor, 12.1 kΩ (R2), from VIOC to FBX sets the LDO drop; 36.5 kΩ (R3) from IN to VIOC sets the input reached when the LT3094 is disabled. The converter output is -4.3 V for a -3.3 V LDO output and -5 V with the LDO disabled.
notes: The LT3094 pins other than IN and VIOC are not part of this circuit.

circuits.title: Parallel devices, 22 µF input (Figure 15)
circuits.description: Two LT3094s share one SET network, 16.5 kΩ with 4.7 µF across it, which with the 200 µA from both SET pins sets -3.3 V. Each output has its own 10 µF capacitor at OUT/OUTS and reaches the common -3.3 V output through a 20 mΩ ballast, so the two share current; together they deliver 1 A from -5 V ±5%. EN/UV and PGFB of both parts go to IN, ILIM of both to ground. The input has one 22 µF capacitor.
notes: PG and VIOC of both parts are left unconnected.

circuits.title: Parallel devices
circuits.description: Two LT3094s share one SET network, 16.5 kΩ with 4.7 µF across it, which with the 200 µA from both SET pins sets -3.3 V. Each output has its own 10 µF capacitor at OUT/OUTS and reaches the common -3.3 V output through a 20 mΩ ballast, so the two share current; together they deliver 1 A from -5 V ±5%. EN/UV and PGFB of both parts go to IN, ILIM of both to ground. The input has one 10 µF capacitor.
notes: PG and VIOC of both parts are left unconnected.

circuits.title: Programming undervoltage lockout
circuits.description: The typical -5 V to -3.3 V regulator with an input undervoltage lockout. REN2 (110 kΩ) from IN to EN/UV and REN1 (49.9 kΩ) from EN/UV to ground turn the part on when the input reaches -4 V and off again at -3.35 V, from VIN(UVLO) = -1.26 V • (1 + 110k/49.9k). PGFB is tied to IN, so fast start-up and power good are off. RSET 33.2 kΩ with 4.7 µF, RILIM 7.5 kΩ, 10 µF at input and output.
notes: PG and VIOC are left unconnected.

circuits.title: Positive and negative variable supply
circuits.description: A 12 V input makes adjustable positive and negative rails of 500 mA each. A dual LT8582 runs channel 1 as a SEPIC (L1, 2.2 µF coupling capacitor, D1) feeding an LT3045-1 positive regulator, and channel 2 as an inverting converter (L2, 2.2 µF, D2) feeding the LT3094. Each LDO's VIOC drives its converter's feedback: a 187 kΩ resistor from the LDO input to VIOC/FBX on the positive side, 14.7 kΩ from VIOC to FBX2 and 187 kΩ from the LDO input to VIOC on the negative side, so each converter tracks its LDO output. Each LDO output is set by a 150 kΩ variable resistor with 4.7 µF across it. 267 kΩ joins VPOS to the LT3094 input and 249 kΩ joins VNEG to the LT3045-1 input. The LT8582 channels run from 80.6 kΩ timing resistors with CLKOUT1 driving SYNC2; each has 0.1 µF soft-start and a 2 kΩ + 47 nF with 100 pF compensation network.
notes: L1 is a DRQ125-8R2 and L2 a DRQ125-4R7 coupled inductor; D1 and D2 are DFLS230L.
The LT3094 PG pin, the LT8582 GATE1, GATE2 and CLKOUT2 pins have no connection.

equations.name: Resistor thermal noise
equations.note: Output noise is the RMS sum of reference current noise times RSET, the error amplifier noise and this resistor noise.

operation.text: A 100 µA zero-TC current reference flows into SET, which is also the error amplifier's inverting input; the resistor from SET to ground turns it into the reference voltage, and the amplifier, a rail-to-rail unity-gain buffer, copies it to OUTS/OUT. Because the gain is always one, loop gain, bandwidth, noise, PSRR and transient response do not depend on the programmed voltage, and load regulation is specified in microvolts rather than as a percentage. The output runs from 0 V (0 Ω at SET) to VIN minus dropout.

An NPN input pair works for outputs from 0 V to -0.8 V and a PNP pair beyond -1.5 V, with a gradual handover between -0.8 V and -1.5 V. The PNP pair gives the best figures; offset, SET current, noise and PSRR change with the active pair.

The SET resistor sets the accuracy, so use a precision part. Any leakage into or out of SET shifts the output: 100 nA is a 0.1 % error. Good insulation (Teflon, Kel-F), flux cleaning and, in humid places, a conformal coat at SET help. A guard ring round SET held near its potential, ideally driven from OUT, on both board sides reduces leakage; wider rings cut bulk leakage more.

operation.topic: SET pin bypass and external drive
operation.text: SET is a high-impedance node and can pick up noise, worst with the minimum output capacitor at heavy load; 10 nF from SET to ground cures it. SET can instead be driven by a voltage source that can supply 100 µA, such as a precision reference, which removes the reference current and resistor tolerances from the output error.

OUTS gives a Kelvin sense of the output and the ground end of the SET resistor a Kelvin sense of the load ground. The regulator's bandwidth is about 1 MHz, close to the roughly 1.6 MHz self-resonance of a 10 µF 1206 ceramic, so tie OUTS straight to COUT, the ground of CSET straight to the ground of COUT, and keep the grounds of CIN and COUT near each other. The part will not oscillate with a poorer layout, but phase margin, noise and PSRR can suffer.

Stability needs at least 10 µF with ESR below 30 mΩ and ESL below 1.5 nH; low-ESR ceramics are recommended. Larger values help only slightly with noise and PSRR because bandwidth falls as capacitance rises, but they do reduce peak deviation in load steps. Decoupling capacitors on the loads add to the output capacitance.

Z5U and Y5V give high capacitance in small cases but lose much of it with bias and temperature: a 16 V 10 µF Y5V on a 5 V rail can fall to 1 µF to 2 µF over temperature. X5R and X7R are steadier (X7R over temperature, X5R cheaper and in larger values) but still lose value under DC bias; larger cases hold value better. The Murata GJ8 series is recommended for its low voltage coefficient in small cases.

Ceramic capacitors can turn vibration or thermal shock into voltage. On the output and input this adds little noise thanks to the low output impedance and high PSRR, but a ceramic SET capacitor can add hundreds of µV peak-to-peak. SET tolerates high ESR and ESL, so a tantalum, electrolytic or film capacitor works there, though electrolytics have high 1/f noise. Surface-mount parts are recommended.

A 10 µF ceramic at IN is enough when the source is close, such as a nearby battery. Long supply leads with a low-ESR input capacitor form a high-Q LC tank that can ring or interact with the regulator; one foot of 30-AWG wire is about 465 nH. Add roughly 1 µF per 6 inches of lead on top of the 10 µF, run supply and return close together (two 30-AWG wires 0.02 inch apart have about one-fifth the inductance of one wire), add 0.1 Ω to 0.5 Ω in series at the cost of dropout, or parallel a higher-ESR tantalum or electrolytic with the 10 µF ceramic. Extra output capacitance also helps but takes far more than extra input capacitance.

After a switching converter, switching current in a capacitor right at IN makes magnetic fields that couple into the output and can cost over 30 dB of PSRR at 1 MHz, even with the regulator removed. The input capacitor can be left off if the converter's output capacitor is more than an inch away; more than a couple of inches away, the missing capacitor can let the part oscillate. The demo board layout keeps the input capacitor while limiting trace inductance and magnetic loops.

Switching edges in the hundreds of MHz pass beyond the regulator's bandwidth almost straight to the output, and the output capacitor's ESL limits how much it absorbs. A ferrite bead, or the inductance of a short trace (about 0.5 inch), with a capacitor that is low impedance at those frequencies forms an LC filter for them.

The reference current has about 27 pA/√Hz of noise (8 nARMS from 10 Hz to 100 kHz); times RSET it adds to the error amplifier noise and the resistor's thermal noise. With no gain from SET to output, a SET capacitor bypasses the reference and resistor noise, leaving the error amplifier: typically 2 nV/√Hz from 1 kHz to 1 MHz and 0.8 µVRMS over 10 Hz to 100 kHz with 4.7 µF at SET, whatever the output voltage. N regulators in parallel cut noise by √N.

Besides lowering noise, CSET improves PSRR and transient response and soft-starts the output, limiting inrush. Its leakage adds DC error (100 nA gives 0.1 %), so a good low-leakage ceramic is recommended.

Low 1/f noise below 100 Hz needs a larger CSET, up to 22 µF, which would make start-up slow. While PGFB is less than -300 mV, the SET current rises to about 1.8 mA, except in current limit, dropout, thermal shutdown or with the input below its minimum. To disable it tie PGFB to IN, or to OUT for outputs beyond -300 mV; this also disables power good.

EN/UV switches the part into a micropower shutdown. The -1.26 V turn-on threshold (215 mV hysteresis) with a divider from the input sets an accurate UVLO. The pin also turns the part on above +1.26 V, so in a bipolar supply the positive rail can sequence the LT3094 on after the positive regulator. Tie EN/UV to IN if unused.

VIOC is a fast unity-gain amplifier output equal to the lower of IN - OUTS or -1.5 V. It goes into the feedback node or divider of an upstream switching regulator and sinks at least 100 µA; it sources current only through its internal impedance to ground, about 40 kΩ ±15%, which matters in a maximum-input configuration or when the part is disabled. A -1 V drop is the suggested balance of dissipation and PSRR; the drop can be programmed between -0.41 V (dropout) and -1.3 V. In a short circuit the loop pulls the converter down and limits dissipation. Phase delay is under 4° up to 100 kHz, so a converter with 50° margin keeps at least 46°; keep VIOC capacitance below 20 pF. With paralleled parts, use one VIOC and float the others. If SET opens, the LDO input would rise to the converter's maximum and could exceed the IN rating; R3 from VIOC to IN sets a maximum.

When PGFB goes below -300 mV the open-collector PG releases to high impedance; the comparator has 7 mV hysteresis and 5 µs deglitching. Power good and fast start-up are disabled for outputs between 0 V and -300 mV. Float PG if unused. PG and PGFB traces running side by side for more than about two inches can couple PG into PGFB and oscillate; keep them apart or use lower divider resistances.

ILIM regulates at -300 mV; the resistor between ILIM and ground fixes the pin current, which sets the limit. Kelvin-connect the resistor to GND. Above 7 V input-to-output, foldback lowers the internal limit, which can override the programmed one to keep the transistor in its safe operating area. Tie ILIM to GND if unused.

After a step from heavy to light or no load the output overshoots and a light load discharges COUT slowly. When OUTS is above SET a current source, typically 3.5 mA, discharges the output; if OUTS is held there externally the source stays on until it is released.

For more current connect every SET pin to one node and every IN pin to another, and join the OUT pins through short PCB traces used as ballast resistors (Table 2). The 2 mV worst-case offset keeps the ballast small: with two parts and 20 mΩ each, sharing is better than 20 % at full load, and at 1 A the ballast adds 10 mV, 0.3 % on -3.3 V. OUTS of each part goes straight to its output capacitor. More than two can be paralleled, which also lowers noise and spreads heat; a series input resistor or one across the regulator also spreads heat at high differential.
Full performance depends on layout; the DC2624A demo board shows the recommended layout.

Thermal shutdown is nominally 165 °C with about 8 °C hysteresis. In continuous use, E- and I-grade parts are limited to a 125 °C junction, H- and MP-grade parts to 150 °C. The exposed pads of both packages connect the die attach to the board; heat spreads through PCB copper, stiffeners and plated through-holes. Tables 3 and 4 give θJA against top copper area.

Safe-operating-area protection lowers current limit above 7 V input-to-output, but some current is available at every differential. At start-up the output follows the input so the differential stays low. At high input with low output and heavy load, for example after a short is removed or with EN/UV raised after the input is up, the load line can cross the current-limit curve twice and the output may stay low until the input is cycled to zero.

Current limit and thermal limit protect against output overloads. Pulling the output above ground does no damage: with IN open or grounded OUT can go 20 V above GND, with up to 25 mA into OUT and out of GND. With IN powered, OUT sinks the foldback short-circuit current and the part protects itself by thermal limiting; grounding EN/UV turns it off and stops the current.
EN/UV, ILIM, PG, PGFB, SET, GND, VIOC, OUTS and OUT each have an internal diode to IN; keep them more positive than IN in operation and never more than 0.3 V below IN in a fault.
